newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO deploys troops as Serb leaders vie for power.
newsitem.headline: NATO deploys troops as Serb leaders vie for power.

text.p: NATO peacekeeping troops stepped up patrols in Bosnia on Wednesday amid a tense power struggle between Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic and her hardline government opponents.

The NATO-led peace force said it had deployed additional troops to the northern industrial town of Banja Luka to prevent possible violence between forces loyal to Plavsic and diehard hardliners loyal to indicted war criminal and ex-president Radovan Karadzic.

"We received indicators overnight of a possible threat to security in the Banja Luka area and we established a military presence in order to maintain a secure environment," spokesman Major Chris Riley told a news conference.
Riley declined to elaborate and said that the unspecified threat had receded on Wednesday.
No shots have been fired so far in the political battle between Karadzic's hardliners, who control a vast police force, and Plavsic, who enjoys the sympathy of some military officers.
Plavsic has vowed to fight "all the way" to stay in power after delivering a blistering condemnation of corrupt hardliners controlling the country's Serb republic.

France became the first country to lend clear public support to Plavsic on Wednesday, saying it could not "tolerate persons indicted by the international criminal tribunal having a role in political life".

Western envoys, who see Plavsic as more cooperative than Karadzic and his allies, fear that her removal would be a blow to efforts to build stability and prevent another war in the former Yugoslav republic.

Karadzic, indicted twice by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, and his allies in the ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) launched fresh attacks on Plavsic through the official media, accusing her of selling out Serb interests to foreign powers.
As British armoured vehicles patrolled Banja Luka, major powers and the international community's High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, met in the Hague to discuss the turmoil.
Plavsic slammed the Serb leadership in a 40-minute television address on Tuesday, saying Karadzic had authorised "shameful" smuggling deals at the expense of ordinary people.

Political sources said Plavsic may have gained access to the airwaves because she enjoyed the sympathy of some officers in the army, which controls the tightly-controlled television system's transmitters.
The army, which Karadzic has tried to purge, has its own grievances against leading SDS politicians whom it accused during the war of rampant corruption.
The Bosnian Serb economy remains firmly under the control of Karadzic and powerful allies who include Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective multi-ethnic presidency.

The conflict between Plavsic and the hardliners has simmered for months as a result of her campaign against corruption and accusations by the SDS that she was being too cooperative with international peacemakers.
It reached a crisis at the weekend when she tried to sack Interior Minister Dragan Kijic for refusing to investigate two suspect companies in which Karadzic and Krajisnik have a stake.

In her speech, she also confirmed the international community's suspicion that Karadzic was still in charge of the Serb government despite efforts to push him out of public life because of his war crimes indictment.
The SDS leadership, accusing Plavsic of overstepping her constitutional prerogatives, has scheduled a meeting of the Bosnian Serb parliament on Friday in an attempt to remove her.
According to the constitution, she cannot be removed by parliament but only by a referendum.
